item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Philip Abner was going right back into the fire.
Abner had just made the wrong kind of history on Friday night, surrendering four homers in one inning. Max Muncy and Kyle Tucker went back-to-back to start the frame, then Mookie Betts and Will Smith did the same later in the inning. Following that disastrous outing, manager Tony Vitello said Abner would “be back out there at some point.”
That “some point” arrived less than 24 hours later. With the game on the line. In front of an announced attendance of 47,410. Considering the circumstances, Vitello’s decision was a true stunner. A night removed from the worst game of his career, Abner had to put out a fire at the game’s most critical point.
If this were Hollywood, maybe Abner would’ve enjoyed his redemption. But redemption never arrived. No feel-good story, no bounceback. Only an agonizing inning and the latest bizarre loss in a season full of them, a 10-4 defeat that had the makings of an upset win against back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner Tarik Subal.
“Just needing to get one out. [He was] our only lefty in the bullpen, needing to get one out,” said manager Tony Vitello of the decision. “Other than our two guys that we want to finish with the game, you saw everybody we had available.”
When the Dodgers’ left-handed-hitting Josue De Paula stepped to the plate with two on and two outs, Abner was the team’s only available left-handed reliever to spell rookie Yunior Marte.
Reiver Sanmartín landed on the injured list before the game. Sam Hentges, who was activated from the injured list before the game, was unavailable, per Vitello. Matt Wilkinson was another option, but “Tugboat” is starting on Sunday. So, Abner.
That said, Vitello wasn’t required to seek out the left-on-left matchup. Especially since Abner had just become the first Giants pitcher to allow at least four homers in one inning since Alan Embree on May 20, 2001.
The hitter before De Paula, Kyle Tucker, was also left-handed, but Vitello left Marte face him. Vitello was likely saving Dylan Smith and Trent Harris for the later innings, but Kuhnel and Duncan Davitt, who he used in the sixth and seventh, were options.
Given how Friday unfolded, Vitello was asked if there was any consideration of steering clear of Abner.
“We avoided [Kyle] Tucker,” Vitello said. “But kind of what we got going on right now is finding out what you can and can’t do. And if I’m in his position, I’m dying to get back out there and see what I can do. I’ve had several guys come in the office, and we’ve had that conversation before. … Maybe we come up with a different plan, but otherwise, looking t get one out right there.” xr
Vitello added: “We talked about it last night and let him know that there’d be an opportunity around the corner. We knew Sanmartín was out. Sam wouldn’t be available based off his routine and his flight schedule and all that. So, we have talked about that.”
Abner’s first pitch foreshadowed what was to come, a bounced curveball that catcher Andrew Knizner couldn’t handle. He walked De Paula on five pitches, loading the bases for switch-hitter Tommy Edman.
Edman, who crushes lefties, pulled a single to left that scored Teoscar Hernández easily. Left fielder Turner Hill’s throw beat Kyle Tucker to the plate but was a tad off line and got away from Knizner. De Paula advanced to third, while Edman took second.
Following Edman’s two-run single, Miguel Rojas emerged from the Dodgers’ bench and rapped a single of his own. De Paula strolled home for Los Angeles’ third run of the inning, but a perfect throw by Hill nabbed Edman at the plate to mercifully end the inning and Abner’s night. Marte finished his night having allowed six runs over 4 2/3 innings.
“That’s just how baseball is,” Abner told this news organization when asked of the last two nights. “There’s too many games. You’re not going to be perfect all year. I definitely haven’t had the year that I’ve wanted. I’ve got one more week, and I’m going to make the most of it. Whatever happens, happens.”
Regarding Friday’s outing, in particular, Abner revealed that he had been tipping his pitches.
“Giving up four home runs sucks. It’s even worse when we were looking at video and found out I was tipping my pitches a little bit and telegraphing every single one of them,” Abner said. “Not even just fastball and offspeed. I worked on what to do to figure that out today. Walking my lefty isn’t exactly a good start, but I appreciate him letting me get back out there as soon as possible. It’s just one of those series. You’re going to have a bad series, and that’s just how it is.”
The bottom of the sixth featured a different flavor of agony as reliever Joel Kuhnel allowed three runs (one earned) due to a pair of misplays.
Shortstop Christian Koss committed an error when he dropped a throw on a force play from first baseman Brett Harris that would’ve been the second out. Two batters later, Harris could’ve been charged with an error after failing to corral a playable scoop from Koss that would’ve ended the inning. De Paula made Harris’ gaffe hurt, immediately driving in two more runs with a single.
The margin of defeat doesn’t reflect the Giants’ feistiness during the game’s first half. Thanks in large part to Victor Bericoto, San Francisco and Los Angeles entered the bottom of the fifth tied 4-4 as the Giants tagged Skubal for four runs.
Bericoto hit a no-doubt, two-run homer off Skubal on a middle-middle fastball in the third, emphatically throwing his bat before rounding the bases. The Giants scored a run in the fourth when Jonah Cox perfectly executed the squeeze play, then another in the fifth when Bericoto and Jung Hoo Lee hit back-to-back doubles, the latter driving in the former.
Then, that fateful bottom of the fifth.
For Skubal, it was the first time he allowed four runs in a game as a Dodger. This month alone, the Giants have scored nine combined runs off Skubal and Paul Skenes, the reigning Cy Young Award winners in both leagues. Despite those efforts, the Giants have lost both games.
Abner, 24, is one of many players fighting for a spot on next year’s roster. Realistically, with 16 players on the 60-day injured list and a wave of cuts coming, Abner could be looking at his final days in San Francisco. Regardless of what’s next, Abner is hoping for the best.
And to put the last two nights behind him.
“I’m definitely hoping they’ll keep me around,” Abner said. “It’s a long offseason. I’m going to do a lot to improve myself, so I’m hoping they’ll take a chance on me and keep it going from there.”

item.title: [MLB.com] These stars have turned their seasons around in the second half
item.dc:creator: Theo DeRosa
item.description: One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run. item.content:encoded:
One well-timed hot streak from a star player can be all a team needs to go on a big run.
While many key contributors struggled in the first half of 2026, several have picked it up big time since the All-Star break, lifting their clubs to late-season success.
Here are 10 players -- five hitters and five pitchers -- who have turned things around in the second half.
All stats are through Saturday's games unless otherwise specified.
Hitters
Alex Bregman, Cubs
For as good as National League MVP Award favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong has been lately, it’s actually Bregman who entered Saturday leading all qualifying hitters with a 168 wRC+ in the second half. The third baseman has a .298/.376/.609 slash line since the All-Star break, with his 17 second-half homers tied for fourth most in MLB.
Batting just .241 with nine home runs and a .695 OPS prior to the break, Bregman hadn’t exactly been meeting expectations after signing a five-year, $175 million deal with the Cubs. Now, though, he is up to 5.1 FanGraphs WAR, his highest total since 2022 (5.4). He’s been a big reason the Cubs are currently on track to host an NL Wild Card Series at Wrigley Field, and he will be a key bat in the middle of Chicago’s lineup in the postseason.
Steven Kwan, Guardians
With this week’s series win over the White Sox, the Guardians have surged into first place in the AL Central, in large part thanks to their leadoff hitter’s resurgence. In addition to his strong defense in left field -- Kwan has won four straight AL Gold Gloves in left to begin his career -- Kwan has been on fire at the plate.
After a disappointing first-half slash line of .225/.332/.282, including a .188 batting average in May, Kwan ranks second among qualifiers with a .347 average and is tied with Yordan Alvarez for first with a .435 on-base percentage in the second half. He has been setting the table admirably for a Cleveland club not getting as much as usual from third baseman José Ramírez (94 wRC+) and could help the Guardians secure not only the division title but a key first-round bye.
Jackson Merrill, Padres
Merrill took a step back in 2025 after finishing second to the Pirates’ Paul Skenes in 2024 NL Rookie of the Year Award voting, and the Padres center fielder appeared headed for further regression based on early returns in 2026. Merrill’s OPS was below .600 in late May as San Diego scuffled offensively, and he took a .219/.278/.350 slash line into the break.
Since then, Merrill has been a major reason why the Padres have a 38-21 (.644) record in the second half, tied with the Brewers for the best in the NL. He’s hitting .312 with 16 home runs, 48 RBIs and a .944 OPS in 59 games in the second half while playing standout defense in center. Merrill’s ability to recapture his rookie form has given the Padres a fighting chance to host a Wild Card Series, and he’ll be a key middle-of-the-order bat for the club.
George Springer, Blue Jays
Springer improved his OPS by nearly 300 points from 2024 to 2025, slashing .309/.399/.560 and finishing seventh in AL MVP balloting as Toronto fell just short of a World Series title. But the veteran’s numbers fell off again early in 2026, especially after Springer returned from a stint on the injured list for a left big toe fracture. He hit just .218 with a .677 OPS before the All-Star break, a period of rest that seemed to help considerably.
Springer recorded multiple hits in five of his first nine second-half games, finishing July with an .878 OPS, before batting .321 with an .858 OPS in August. While he has slowed a bit in September, battling multiple injuries, he has clearly found his footing at the plate. It might not be enough to drag a Blue Jays team dealing with a host of pitching injuries and a down year from Vladimir Guerrero Jr. to the postseason, but Toronto -- three games out of an AL Wild Card spot -- still has a chance.
Fernando Tatis Jr., Padres
While Merrill’s turnaround has been integral to the Padres’ second-half surge, Tatis’ production out of the leadoff spot has perhaps been even more important. The three-time All-Star began the season by scorching the baseball into the ground, going 55 games before hitting his first home run of the year on May 30.
The second half brought on a true power surge for Tatis, who homered three times in his first four games after the All-Star break and is now up to 24 dingers on the season. Entering Saturday, his 167 wRC+ in the second half was second in MLB, behind only Bregman. Tatis has raised his season OPS to .819 and has given the Padres a dangerous option at leadoff down the stretch.
Pitchers
Brayan Bello, Red Sox
Bello has turned the page on a dismal start to the season. The right-hander, coming off a 3.35 ERA as a starter in 2025, had a 9.00 ERA in his first six starts of 2026 and was moved to a bulk-relief role. Still, Bello took a 6.06 ERA into the All-Star break as the Red Sox finally began to heat up, winning nine straight games to end the first half and extending the streak to a franchise record-tying 15.
Bello has continued to impress for Boston, earning the start on Saturday and baffling the Rays over eight innings of one-run ball with 11 strikeouts. In the midst of a statistically unprecedented season, he’s found something that works, which has been crucial for a Red Sox team that has surged into postseason position and appears headed for another clash with the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series.
Robert Gasser, Brewers
Tommy John surgery in June 2024 cut short Gasser’s promising rookie season, but he returned to make two solid starts at the tail end of 2025. The left-hander couldn’t sustain that success early in 2026, taking a 5.24 ERA into the All-Star break after being tagged for seven runs in three innings in his final first-half start.
Since then, Gasser has a 3.00 ERA in 57 innings of work after holding the Orioles scoreless over seven excellent innings on Saturday in Baltimore. In his first four September outings, including two against the Cubs, he has allowed just four earned runs across 21 innings pitched. With Brandon Woodruff’s 2026 return questionable and Kyle Harrison struggling mightily, Gasser’s improvement has made him an important arm for a Milwaukee team fighting to secure the NL’s No. 1 seed.
Tyler Mahle, Braves
Mahle owned a 5.13 ERA through his first 18 starts of 2026 for the Giants, but the Braves saw something in the veteran right-hander. Atlanta acquired Mahle ahead of the Trade Deadline for righty reliever Anthony Molina in a move that has paid considerable dividends for the Braves’ battered rotation.
Mahle has allowed only seven earned runs in eight starts for Atlanta, completing six or more innings in all but one of those outings. His 1.28 ERA in that span is the third best among all pitchers (min. 40 innings), and he’s been an excellent complement to ace lefty Chris Sale atop the Braves rotation. With Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Bryce Elder, Reynaldo López and Hurston Waldrep all on the injured list, Mahle has not only covered important innings but has been remarkably effective.
Aaron Nola, Phillies
Nola had an ERA above 6 in an injury-marred 2025 season, and his 2026 looked to be more of the same. The usually dependable right-hander gave up 20 home runs in the first half alone, tied for the fifth most in MLB, and headed into the All-Star break with a 5.75 ERA.
Since then, Nola has returned to near-vintage form for the Phillies, who have also gotten strong second halves from lefty Jesús Luzardo (currently on the injured list with left shoulder inflammation) and rookie righty Andrew Painter. After Thursday’s excellent start against the Mets, Nola has a 2.78 ERA in the second half, striking out 67 in 71 1/3 innings despite giving up 14 more home runs in just 12 starts. If he can limit the long balls, he could be at least an adequate replacement for Luzardo if the southpaw cannot return for the start of the postseason.
Brandon Pfaadt, D-backs
Pfaadt hasn’t quite lived up to his billing as a former top prospect just yet, but he’s shown flashes, such as his success against the Dodgers and Phillies during the D-backs’ 2023 World Series run. The righty's recent results have been quite encouraging, too: Pfaadt has a 3.01 ERA in the second half, including a run of 27 2/3 scoreless innings across four starts from July 28-Aug. 14. 
Optioned to Triple-A Reno in June after a poor start to the year, Pfaadt now has the chance to help pitch the D-backs into the playoffs, which might be difficult in an NL Wild Card race featuring the Cubs, Phillies and Padres. Pfaadt is lined up to start during Arizona’s final series of the season, a pivotal three-game set in San Diego from Sept. 25-27, and his outing could determine the D-backs’ postseason fate.

item.dc:creator: John Perrotto

item.content:encoded:
Garcia is thankful to be back in the starting lineup for the final days of the 2026 regular season. He has been limited to just 76 games, because of a partial tear of his left hamstring and just returned from the injured list on Tuesday after missing 21 games.
“I didn’t think I might play again this year, so I’m thankful,” Garcia said following Friday night’s 8-5 loss to the Pirates to open a three-game series at PNC Park. “I just wish there were more games left.”
Garcia had high hopes for 2026 after making his first All-Star Game appearance last season, then signing a five-year, $57.5 million contract extension that runs through 2030 and includes a club option for ‘31.
Alas, Garcia is slashing .262/.318/.378 with three home runs.
However, the 26-year-old provided a bright spot against Pittsburgh in what turned out to be a frustrating night for Kansas City. Garcia’s two-run double in the third inning helped the Royals build a 4-0 lead against reigning National League Cy Young winner Paul Skenes.
Still, they eventually lost for the 12th time in their last 17 games despite home runs by Vinnie Pasquantino and Michael Massey.
“We think the world of Mikey,” manager Matt Quatraro said of Garcia. “We committed a lot of years and a lot of money to him, because we think he’s a really good player who can help us win. Getting him back on the field is important for us, and it’s good for him, too.
“He probably thought his season was over, but he worked very hard through the rehab process to get back. And he got a big hit in a big spot.”
Just eight games remain for the Royals, so there isn’t a whole lot of season left to salvage for Garcia. Yet, he appreciates what few days remain and getting a big hit off a Cy Young winner.
“I like to face the best pitchers,” Garcia said with a smile. “It makes me fight that much harder. It felt really good to get a big hit there with a couple of guys on base. It’s been a tough year for me personally, but we have come back here, we want to finish the season healthy, and we want to help the team win some games. I want to go home for the winter with a good feeling.”
The usually unflappable Randy Dobnak admittedly was fighting some feelings when he took the mound in his hometown for just the second time in his career. The right-hander grew up in suburban South Park, Pa.
Dobnak’s previous appearance at PNC Park came with the Twins in 2020. However, fans weren’t permitted to attend games during that pandemic-shortened season. Dobnak estimated he had at least 200 family members and friends in the stands and had attended approximately 300 games in this ballpark.
“This was really kind of special,” Dobnak said. “After I threw my last warm-up pitch, I stood there on the mound and took it all in. Growing up, this was the place I always wanted to be. I caught myself almost getting a little bit emotional out there.”
Dobnak paused and chuckled.
“That quickly changed when I threw my first pitch and [Konnor] Griffin singled right back up the middle,” he said.
Unfortunately for Dobnak and his throng of supporters, that signaled what was to come. He lasted just 3 2/3 innings and gave up four runs on seven hits and two walks, while striking out one.
Dobnak left with a 5-3 lead, but the Pirates rallied against the Royals’ bullpen. Spencer Horwitz’s two-run single off Nate Pearson in a three-run seventh inning broke a 5-5 tie.
“I think the biggest thing was first-pitch strikes with Randy,” Quatraro said. “It was an interesting game for him. There were four hits down the third-base line from a left-handed hitter and a couple of infield hits. He had a lot of traffic to deal with.”

item.content:encoded:
Livvy Dunne Dismisses Fantasy Baseball Manager's Paul Skenes Request With 'South Park' Meme
Don't bother Livvy Dunne with complaints about how Paul Skenes is impacting your fantasy baseball team.
After Dunne posted a TikTok video showing her doing gymnastics exercises, a fan in the comments decided to write a snarky message asking her to tell Skenes to "do good for my fantasy" team.
Rather than let the message slide, Dunne replied with a South Park meme featuring Stan saying "Dude, we don't care."

It's hard to argue Skenes hasn't helped fantasy teams this season. He's obviously not pitching as well as he did in 2024 or 2025, but his 3.78 ERA and 185 strikeouts in 162 innings is far from terrible.
Sure, Skenes only ranks 32nd among all starting pitchers in total fantasy points entering Friday. He is right around Tarik Skubal, Jacob deGrom and Nolan McLean.
This has been a strange season for many pitchers. Not many people would have guessed in April that Jesús Luzardo, Drew Rasmussen and Parker Messick were going to be top-eight fantasy starters.
